## Warm-Up: Quick Concept and Calculation Checks

a. A country's real GDP per capita grows at 2.5 percent per year. Using the Rule of 70,
   approximately how many years will it take to double?
b. A country's real GDP per capita grows at 5 percent per year instead. Approximately how many
   years will it take to double?
c. For each, say whether it is a *supply* factor, the *demand* factor, or the *efficiency* factor
   in economic growth: (i) a country discovers a large new oil field, (ii) total spending in the
   economy is too low to buy up all the goods the economy is capable of producing, (iii) a factory
   switches from an outdated, high-cost production method to a modern, lower-cost one.
d. In a given year, hours worked in an economy grow 0.8 percent and labor productivity (output per
   hour) grows 2.1 percent. Approximately what is the growth rate of real GDP?
e. Rank these contributors to U.S. productivity growth from *most* to *least* quantitatively
   important, according to growth accounting studies: education and training, technological
   advance, capital per worker (capital deepening), economies of scale and improved resource
   allocation.
f. True or False: a positive relationship between a nation's productivity growth rate and its
   average real hourly wage growth rate exists because competitive labor markets tend to pay
   workers according to what they produce.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. $70 / 2.5 = 28$ years.
b. $70 / 5 = 14$ years.
c. (i) *Supply factor* (more natural resources). (ii) *Demand factor* (total spending must be
   enough to purchase the expanding potential output). (iii) *Efficiency factor* (using resources
   at their lowest-cost combination, productive efficiency).
d. Approximately $0.8 + 2.1 = 2.9$ percent (labor input growth plus productivity growth).
e. Largest to smallest: technological advance, capital per worker, education and training,
   economies of scale and improved resource allocation.
f. *True.*

</details>

## Problem 1: Small Growth Differences, Compounded

Country A and Country B both start with real GDP per capita of $8,000. Country A grows at 2
percent per year. Country B grows at 4 percent per year.

a. Using the Rule of 70, how many years does it take each country to double its GDP per capita?
b. Estimate each country's real GDP per capita after 35 years by compounding the growth rate year
   by year.
c. How many times larger is Country B's GDP per capita than Country A's after 35 years?
d. Both countries started at the same GDP per capita and neither growth rate sounds dramatic in a
   single year. What does this problem illustrate about long-run growth?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"

years = list(range(36))
a = [8000 * (1.02 ** y) for y in years]
b = [8000 * (1.04 ** y) for y in years]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=a, mode="lines", name="Country A (2% growth)",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
                          hovertemplate="Year %{x}<br>$%{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=b, mode="lines", name="Country B (4% growth)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3),
                          hovertemplate="Year %{x}<br>$%{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>"))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Years", yaxis_title="Real GDP per capita",
    width=600, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.02, y=1.15, orientation="h")
)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", tickformat="$,.0f")
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.show()
```

a. Country A: $70/2 = 35$ years. Country B: $70/4 = 17.5$ years.
b. Country A: $8{,}000 \times 1.02^{35} \approx \$16{,}000$. Country B:
   $8{,}000 \times 1.04^{35} \approx \$31{,}600$.
c. $31{,}600 / 16{,}000 \approx 2.0$, Country B's GDP per capita is about *twice* Country A's after
   35 years, even though B's doubling time is only half of A's.
d. A growth rate that looks small year to year, a gap of just 2 percentage points here, compounds
   into an enormous difference in living standards over a working lifetime. This is exactly why
   economists care so much about small, sustained differences in growth rates rather than dismissing
   them as trivial.

</details>

## Problem 2: Where Does Growth Come From?

An economy's real GDP grew by approximately 3.2 percent over one year. Economists estimate that
total hours worked in the economy grew by 0.9 percent over the same year.

a. Approximately what was the growth rate of labor productivity (output per hour) that year?
b. If, instead, hours worked had *fallen* by 0.4 percent while real GDP still grew 3.2 percent,
   approximately what would labor productivity growth have been?
c. In part (b), the economy produced more total output with *fewer* hours worked. What does that
   imply about labor productivity, and why might that be a healthier long-run growth pattern than
   growth driven mainly by more hours worked?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. Real GDP growth is approximately labor input growth plus productivity growth, so
   $3.2 - 0.9 = 2.3$ percent productivity growth.
b. $3.2 - (-0.4) = 3.6$ percent productivity growth.
c. It implies productivity grew *faster* than total output, each hour worked produced
   substantially more. Growth driven by rising productivity can continue indefinitely as workers
   and firms find better technology, tools, and methods, while growth driven mainly by working more
   hours runs into a hard limit, there are only so many hours in a day and so many working-age
   people. Sustained increases in living standards ultimately depend on productivity growth, not
   on people simply working more.

</details>

## Problem 3: Is Faster Growth Always Better?

A country is debating a policy that would raise its long-run real GDP growth rate from 2.0 percent
to 3.0 percent per year, mainly by encouraging more saving, investment in new capital, and faster
adoption of new technology.

a. Using the Rule of 70, how much sooner would the country's GDP per capita double under the
   faster growth rate?
b. Name one real resource cost this faster growth might require *today*, connecting back to the
   Chapter 6 saving and investment tradeoff.
c. Suppose the policy succeeds in raising average GDP per capita, but nearly all of the additional
   growth goes to the top of the income distribution. Connecting back to Chapter 6, why might the
   *typical* household not feel much better off, even though the national statistics look better?
d. Name one non-income cost that faster growth might impose that GDP per capita does not capture
   at all.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. Doubling time at 2 percent: $70/2 = 35$ years. At 3 percent: $70/3 \approx 23.3$ years. The
   faster growth rate would cut the doubling time by roughly 12 years.
b. More investment in new capital means *less current consumption*, resources devoted to building
   factories, machines, and infrastructure today are resources not used to produce consumer goods
   today. That is the same saving-versus-consumption tradeoff from Chapter 6.
c. GDP per capita is a *mean*. If growth is concentrated among a small share of households, the
   mean can rise substantially while the *median* household's income barely changes, the same
   mean-versus-median gap discussed in Chapter 6.
d. Any reasonable answer describing an externality or nonmarket cost is acceptable, for example:
   environmental damage from more production, resource depletion, or less leisure time if the
   faster growth comes from working more rather than working smarter.

</details>
